Harappa. One of the two major cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, flourishing around twenty-six hundred to nineteen hundred BCE in what is now Pakistan. Comparable in sophistication to its sister city Mohenjo-daro, Harappa gave its name to the entire civilization, which is sometimes called the Harappan culture. Archaeological evidence reveals advanced urban planning, standardized weights and measures, and an undeciphered writing system. Despite centuries of excavation, Harappa remains one of history's most enigmatic civilizations, rivaling ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia in organizational complexity yet leaving minimal records of political or religious structures.

Located in the Punjab region of modern-day Pakistan along the Ravi River, a tributary of the Indus, Harappa was one of the largest settlements of the Indus Valley Civilization. At its height, it had an estimated population of thirty to forty thousand. It featured a planned grid layout with streets oriented to cardinal directions, brick construction, and sophisticated drainage systems. The civilization is often called Harappan culture because Harappa was excavated first and gave the culture its name. The city contained manufacturing areas, suggesting craft specialization in pottery, tools, beads, and seals. Seals with undeciphered writing suggest literacy and record-keeping, but the script remains one of archaeology's great unsolved puzzles.

Harappa showed evidence of extensive trade networks linking it to Mesopotamia, Persia, and the Arabian Peninsula. It declined around nineteen hundred BCE due to unknown causes, possibly environmental change or external pressure, though much remains mysterious about its collapse. Standardized weights and measures across the civilization suggest coordinated trade and a common administrative system. Public baths and reservoirs indicate sophisticated urban infrastructure and hydraulic engineering. The absence of palaces and temples suggests a more egalitarian society compared to contemporary Mesopotamian city-states, though scholarly debate continues about this interpretation.
